transcript.text: My indesit washing machine fills with water and drains but the drum just doesn't go round at all. Its an IWC something. Had it about 9 years. Is it worth fixing?

It may well be worth fixing at nine years, particularly if it proves to be a belt or (on a brushed-motor version) carbon brushes; those are usually more economical repairs than a motor or control-board fault. As it fills and drains but never turns, the main possibilities are a slipped/broken drive belt, worn brushes/motor fault, or less commonly a drum that has become mechanically tight. With it switched off at the socket and unplugged, turn the empty drum by hand: it should feel smooth rather than stiff, rough or grinding. Then, with the covers left on, try a spin-only programme and listen from outside: does it make a motor hum/attempt to run while the drum stays still, or is there no motor sound at all? That distinction is the quickest way to judge the likely repair and whether it is worthwhile.

Thanks. I turned the empty drum by hand with it unplugged and it turns freely and quietly, no scraping or rumble. On a spin-only programme I can hear relays clicking but no motor noise at all. Also, a few weeks ago I noticed a faint hot electrical smell once, but not since.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Do not use the machine again until it has been checked by a qualified engineer, because of the electrical smell. A freely turning drum rules out seized bearings, and relay clicks with no motor sound makes a motor-circuit fault more likely than a simple loading or drainage issue. On an older Indesit this can be worn carbon brushes if it has a brushed motor, but a failed motor connection, motor itself, or the control module can give the same result; a slipped belt remains possible but is less convincing without any attempted motor sound. It can still be worth a diagnostic visit, as brushes or a belt are often viable repairs, whereas a motor/control-board repair may be harder to justify at nine years old. The full model number will help establish the likely motor type and narrow the repair outlook.

candidates: Drive belt off, loose or broken (medium)
Worn motor carbon brushes or motor/control fault (medium)
Drum mechanically tight or bearing fault (low)
